column3: It closely repeats the objection that scattered bones cannot be raised in a new creation and identifies it as disbelief in the signs.
It directly states the earth-to-earth-to-emergence sequence that answers the claim of being lost in the earth.
The disbelievers are driven toward the caller on a hard day, supplying the realized encounter that the focus denies.
It nearly restates the focus: becoming dust, a new creation, and disbelief in the Lord are joined together.
The demand to know when the decision will come continues the same surah's denial of a future divine reckoning.
Its address to the astray deniers supports the focus's diagnosis of a denial disguised as an objection.
It directly parallels the question whether bones and fragments can be raised in a new creation.
It answers the renewed-creation objection by denying any failure in the first creation and locating confusion in the deniers.
The distinction between the Creator and one unable to create only broadly supports confidence in renewed creation.
It repeats the claim that complete dismemberment makes a new creation implausible.
The lesser punishment is meant to bring them back, framing the focus's denial within the surah's warning of consequence.
It explicitly joins disbelief in God's signs with disbelief in meeting Him and its painful consequence.
It directly voices the objection that death, dust, and bones cannot lead to later requital.
God's possession of the earth and what lies beneath it only distantly answers the claim that the buried are lost.
Its mistaken claim of being lost uses similar language but concerns a garden, not burial or resurrection.
It directly asks whether those dead and reduced to dust and bones will be resurrected.
The same surah states that belief at the decisive opening will no longer benefit the disbelievers.
It explicitly connects denial of the signs and the meeting of the Hereafter with being brought into punishment.
A contentious comparison between deities does not clarify burial, renewed creation, or meeting the Lord.
Creation is declared purposeful rather than play, supporting the focus's implied accountability beyond material dissolution.
The disappearance of false intermediaries at need is only a loose parallel to being lost and facing divine judgment.
Its uncertainty about what is intended for those on earth does not illuminate resurrection or the denied meeting.
The same surah presents repeated return to the Fire as the consequence for those who denied its warning.
The challenge over who creates supports the premise that the Creator can establish life beyond its material stages.
It explicitly speaks of bringing a new creation, though its replacement setting is not the focus's individual resurrection question.
Creation in truth supplies a purpose-and-accountability frame for the focus's rejected meeting with the Lord.
The creation of humanity from material substance supports the wider claim that bodily formation is within divine power.
It joins purposeful creation, an appointed term, and widespread disbelief in meeting the Lord.
The immediate continuation answers the focus by stating that death is followed by return to the Lord.
Its declaration of manifest error concerns idolatry and only broadly overlaps the focus's language of being lost.
Guidance and mercy are given so that people may believe in meeting their Lord, directly opposing the focus's disbelief.
The same surah's warning context gives local background but does not itself explain the resurrection objection.
Its use of new formations in mountains is a lexical parallel without a clear resurrection or judgment connection.
It joins the creation of heaven and earth with removal and the bringing of a new creation.
It identifies denial of the Hereafter as the deeper error behind the surrounding mockery of renewed creation.
The ordered creation of the heavens provides only a broad appeal to the Creator's coherent power.
Its confession of manifest error uses the same root but does not concern disappearance in earth or resurrection.
The same surah makes the final filling of Hell the consequence of the divine word, extending the focus's denial toward judgment.
The image of disbelievers rushing forward does not clarify why they reject renewed creation or meeting the Lord.
The accusation of an old error in a family dispute has no material connection to the focus.
They acknowledge God as Creator yet are turned away, exposing the inconsistency behind the focus's denial.
Calling believers astray is a remote use of the lost-language and lacks the focus's resurrection setting.
Turning away from the Lord's remembrance is related disbelief but does not develop the stated objection.
Its possible meeting with Moses or the Book is too ambiguous to clarify meeting the Lord after death.
The earth casting out what it contains offers an image of buried contents emerging for the final encounter.
It explicitly describes those who deny meeting God being overtaken by the Hour and regretting their loss.
The source of the Book does not clarify the focus's burial, new-creation, or meeting claim.
Certainty of meeting the Lord and returning to Him supplies the contrary conviction to the focus's disbelief.
It presents the recurrent response of affluent communities who reject the message sent to them.
The hidden reward in the same surah supplies an outcome context but does not explain the resurrection objection.
A family's mistaken accusation of their father being astray is unrelated to the focus's claim.
Cosmic order, appointed terms, and explained signs are presented so that people become certain of meeting their Lord.
Purposeful creation with an appointed term, followed by disbelievers turning from warning, strongly frames the focus's denial.
Its reminder of human creation supports divine power only in a general way.
Gathering, recognition, and loss through denying meeting God directly describe the encounter the focus rejects.
The nearby pious response gives local contrast but adds little to the focus's specific objection.
It states that disbelievers are repaid for what they did, supplying the accountability denied in the focus.
It explicitly identifies people who reject the Hereafter, though it does not address renewed creation.
Noah's deliverance and the ark as a sign do not clarify this resurrection or meeting claim.
Being found lost and guided uses related language but concerns guidance rather than bodily disappearance.
The elite both disbelieve in the meeting of the Hereafter and dismiss a messenger on account of his human nature.
The immediate sequel shows the criminals before their Lord asking to be returned after seeing and hearing the truth.
Its false inventions vanish from the people who have lost themselves, reinforcing the focus's diagnosis of misdirected denial.
Past peoples reject their messengers and declare doubt, providing a broader pattern for the focus's skeptical speech.
The Creator of earth and high heavens is named as the source of revelation, offering only general support for divine power.
The command not to despair while seeking Joseph does not clarify resurrection or meeting the Lord.
It describes a community that disbelieves in God and the Hereafter, but lacks the focus's specific question.
It explicitly directs people to observe the first creation and concludes that God will produce the final creation.
It directly states that creating and resurrecting all people is like creating and resurrecting a single soul.
Their repeated rejection of revelation illustrates entrenched disbelief but not the focus's resurrection objection.
Human and animal diversity and reverent knowledge do not directly illuminate renewed creation or the final meeting.
God's creation of people and what they make gives only a general premise of divine creative power.
God stands over every soul for what it earns, directly supporting personal accountability before Him.
The frustration of a hostile plan uses related lost-language but has no resurrection or meeting connection.
It combines blocking God's path with disbelief in the Hereafter, a related pattern of refusal.
Its changing posture in human encounters is not the final meeting with the Lord in the focus.
The heavens, angels, and people on earth form a cosmic scene but do not explain the resurrection objection.
Punishment for disbelief is related consequence language but does not clarify the focus's central claims.
Its disbelief and corruption on earth are too remote from being buried, recreated, and meeting the Lord.
At the final confrontation, claimed partners reject their worshipers' account, illustrating a forced encounter exposing false claims.
Being led astray by majority conjecture is a general guidance warning, not an explanation of the focus.
The alleged partners are found lost when confronted, exposing the collapse of the deniers' former account.
It directly repeats the question whether death, dust, and bones will be followed by resurrection.
Those who disbelieve and block God's path have their deeds rendered lost, a consequence parallel to their misdirection.
A denial of corruption and theft in Egypt does not clarify the focus ayah.
The denial that the messenger is astray only loosely contrasts with the focus's use of lostness.
It directly records the objection that death, dust, and bones cannot lead to resurrection.
The messenger's great character does not explain burial, renewed creation, or meeting the Lord.
The fulfilled promise and inheritance of the earth portray the positive outcome of the final divine judgment.
The disbelievers' amazement at a warner introduces the same skeptical setting developed in the following resurrection argument.
It portrays people exposed to punishment on the Day of Resurrection after losing themselves and their families.
It explicitly describes a person as being in far error at the judgment scene, where the truth can no longer be evaded.
It answers doubt about resurrection through successive human formation and the revival of apparently dead earth.
Their admission that the Mighty, Knowing One created heaven and earth challenges their refusal to follow creation's implication.
Mockery in response to the warning supplies the dismissive posture that accompanies the focus's resurrection objection.
Deliverance from a disbelieving people has only a broad relation to the focus's description of disbelief.
The shaking of earth and mountains gives an end-time scene in which the present material order is not final.
It challenges an unsupported claim about angelic creation but does not clarify human resurrection or meeting the Lord.
God's exhaustive knowledge of what is hidden in land and earth counters the suggestion that disappearance makes a person unknowable.
Human creation from water and God's power over its ordered development provide a general premise for renewed formation.
It explicitly traces death, life, death, renewed life, and final return to God.
It directly asks how God gives life to a dead place and answers through a witnessed restoration.
The restoration of the birds gives a concrete demonstration of divine power to revive the dead.
Every soul's death and full recompense on the Day of Resurrection frame the meeting denied in the focus.
It voices the denial that there is anything beyond worldly life or any later resurrection.
It states that God will raise the dead and bring them back to Him.
God brings the living from the dead and the dead from the living, supporting the focus's rejected reversal.
It states that people live, die, and are brought forth from the earth.
The revival of dead land is made a sign of the resurrection of the dead.
It states that all return to God, who begins creation and then repeats it for just recompense.
It asks who begins creation and then repeats it, directly rebutting doubt about renewed creation.
God gives life and death, and people are returned to Him.
It directly records the oath that God will not resurrect the dead and rejects that claim.
It answers the resurrection objection even if people become stone or iron.
It asks who will restore them and answers: the One who created them the first time.
It describes the divine call to which the dead will respond, followed by return to God.
The sleepers' discovery establishes that God's promise and the Hour are without doubt.
The earth is cleared and all people are gathered before God, completing the focus's denied encounter.
It directly voices the question whether a person will be brought forth alive after dying.
It answers resurrection doubt by recalling that God created the person when he was nothing.
It declares that creation will be repeated just as it was first begun.
It states that God gives life to the dead and has power over all things.
It states that the Hour will come and that God will raise those in the graves.
It states that God gives life, causes death, and gives life again.
It states that people die after their present life.
It directly states that people will be resurrected on the Day of Resurrection.
It repeats the objection that after death and becoming dust and bones people will be brought forth.
It voices the denial that there is any life beyond the present world or any resurrection.
Purposeful creation and return to God directly oppose the focus's materialist objection and denied meeting.
False gods are unable to control death, life, or resurrection, reinforcing that these belong to God alone.
It asks who begins creation and then repeats it, directly matching the renewed-creation issue.
It directly repeats the objection that becoming dust with one's forefathers could lead to being brought forth.
It explicitly points to God's beginning of creation and then repeating it.
Every soul will taste death and then return to God.
It directly states that God begins creation, repeats it, and then people return to Him.
It joins bringing life from death, bringing death from life, reviving the earth, and people's emergence from it.
It states that God begins creation and then repeats it, declaring this easier for Him.
The revival of earth after its death is explicitly extended to God's giving life to the dead.
It compares God reviving dead land with the resurrection of the dead.
Dead earth brought to life and made productive gives a direct earthly sign of resurrection.
The trumpet is blown and people emerge from graves and hasten toward their Lord.
Those raised from their resting place recognize the promised encounter as the truth.
It identifies the question of who can revive decayed bones after recalling human creation from a drop.
It directly voices the challenge of who will give life to bones when they have decayed.
It answers that the One who created the bones first will give them life again.
It directly asks whether people and their forefathers will be resurrected.
The trumpet scene depicts death, renewed rising, and people standing to await judgment.
It traces human formation from dust through life and death, ending in a stated return to life.
The revival of barren earth is explicitly made evidence that God gives life to the dead.
God's revival of earth after its death supports His power to revive the dead.
The revival of dead land is followed by the explicit statement that people will likewise be brought forth.
It records the claim that only worldly life and death exist and that there will be no resurrection.
God gives life, causes death, and will gather all people for the Day of Resurrection without doubt.
The Creator of the heavens and earth is explicitly said to be able to give life to the dead.
It directly voices astonishment that death and becoming dust could be followed by a return.
It answers that God knows what the earth diminishes from bodies and preserves it in a record.
Rain revives dead land, supplying a recurring sign of the same divine power.
The revival of a dead land is explicitly compared to emergence from the graves.
It states that the second creation belongs to God.
The declaration that God created people challenges their refusal to affirm the Creator's power.
God determines death and declares His power to replace people and produce them in an unknown form.
Knowledge of the first creation is presented as grounds for remembering its implication.
It directly records the claim that people will never be resurrected and decisively rejects it.
It directly asks whether people think God will not reassemble their bones.
It answers that God can restore even the finest details of a person's form.
The One who formed a human from a drop is declared able to give life to the dead.
It directly records the question whether people will be returned to their former state.
It specifies the objection that this return would occur after becoming decayed bones.
It answers that the return follows a single overwhelming cry.
It states that they will then be on the open plain.
It depicts the graves being overturned, directly answering the claim that the buried remain lost.
The earth is spread out in the final upheaval that immediately precedes its casting out of contents.
It states that God is fully able to return the human being.
The earth casts out its burdens, directly countering the idea that what enters it is permanently lost.
